=== brindle-docs-3.2.md
# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

=== quarrel-docs-1.4.md
# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

# "Quarrel is 3x faster than Brindle" — Quarrel Inc. engineering blog

We published 10 million 1 KB messages through Quarrel 1.4 and Brindle 3.2 on our own c7-metal test rig.
Quarrel reached 3.1 million messages per second, Brindle 1.0 million.

Method notes: one run per library, default settings, the Brindle WAL interval left at its default. The rig and the
harness are not public.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits, as long as you configure it for ordering. Brindle doesn't fit.**

**Brindle 3.2 is out.** Each consumer can hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops the oldest one. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told; the only trace is the `brindle_dropped_total` counter. That breaks your "never lose silently" requirement. Raising `max_unacked` (the cap is 50,000) only moves the limit. Two more problems:
- Ordering only holds per queue when there is a single writer.
- Queues live in memory and are written to the log every 200 ms. The docs don't say what a crash loses, but that window looks like a possible gap.

**Quarrel 1.4 fits, with two conditions:**
- **Ordering:** by default, order is kept only within each of the queue's 64 partitions, not across the whole queue. To get strict order per queue, give every message in a queue the same `partition_key`, such as the queue name. Everything in that queue then goes to one partition, so it loses parallelism.
- **No silent loss:** when a buffer is full, publishers block instead of dropping messages. Unacknowledged messages are delivered again after `ack_timeout` (30 s by default). That means you'll get duplicates, so consumers must be idempotent. A redelivered message may also arrive after later ones, and the docs don't address that, so check it.

**What I didn't count as evidence:**
- **The "3x faster" benchmark:** Quarrel's own vendor wrote it, with one run per library on a test setup nobody else can see. It also says nothing about ordering or loss.
- **The forum post:** it's an anonymous claim, and the poster said they had no data to back it.

I saved what the Brindle docs, Quarrel docs and the benchmark say to the research shelf in memory.
